title: Doubting God's Presence
english: God is patient with those who are failing, and as we reflect on the events that have occurred, the mystery of what happened would become clearer to us.
Having passed over the account of the quail and the manna, it is clear that Israel was hardened and pleasure-loving, not moderately so.

The congregation of the sons of Israel departed from the wilderness of Sin, according to the word of the Lord, and they camped in Rephidim, where they found themselves without water to drink (Exodus 17:1).

The people quarreled with Moses, asking him to give them water to drink, and Moses, in turn, asked them why they were quarreling with him and testing the Lord, saying, 'Why do you quarrel with me, and why do you test the Lord?' (Exodus 17:2).

The people thirsted for water, and they grumbled against Moses, saying that he had brought them up from Egypt to kill them and their children and livestock with thirst, asking, 'Why did you bring us up from Egypt to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?' (Exodus 17:3).

Moses cried out to the Lord, saying that he did not know what to do with the people, as they were on the verge of stoning him, and the Lord instructed Moses to go ahead of the people, taking some of the elders and the staff with which he had struck the river, and to strike the rock in Horeb, from which water would come out for the people to drink (Exodus 17:5-6).

Moses did as he was instructed, and he named the place Temptation and Quarreling, because of the quarreling of the sons of Israel and their testing of the Lord, saying, 'Is the Lord among us or not?' (Exodus 17:7).
In the book of Exodus, we find an oracle that speaks to the issue of the Lord's presence among us (Exodus 17:1-7).
The scripture tells us that the sons of Israel came to the desert of Sin, and the people stayed in Kadesh, where Miriam died and was buried (Numbers 20:1).

However, there was no water for the congregation, and they gathered against Moses and Aaron, reviling them and saying that they wished they had died with their brothers before the Lord, asking, 'Would that we had died in the Lord's presence with our brothers!' (Numbers 20:3).

They asked why Moses had brought them to the desert to kill them and their children, and why they had been led out of Egypt to a bad place without any of the necessities of life, such as seed, or figs, or vines, or streams, or even water to drink, saying, 'Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to this evil place, without seed, or figs, or vines, or pomegranates, without even water to drink?' (Numbers 20:5).
In response to this crisis, Moses and Aaron went from the presence of the congregation to the door of the tent of testimony (Numbers 20:6).
As we examine each event carefully and thoroughly, we gain a typological understanding of the things that happened long ago, and we also appreciate the beauty of spiritual contemplation.
The people's question, 'Is the Lord among us or not?' is a direct quote from the biblical account (Exodus 17:7).
Moses and the people were struggling with the idea of God's presence, as expressed in their question, 'Is the Lord among us or not?'

title: Divine Revelation of the Hidden Mystery of Christ
english: Truly, the mystery of Christ is hard to grasp, and darkness itself would point to it. Indeed, the blessed David, understanding it as I do, had already cried out in anticipation. He made darkness a hiding place around him, his tent encircling him; dark water in the clouds above. From his presence, the brightness caused the clouds to pass through. For Christ's mystery is so hidden that it requires initiation from above and revelation from God. Peter heard this well, understanding the God who was manifested in the flesh as the true Word and Son. Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. Paul likewise affirmed to himself the mystery according to God's revelation. Thus, the imperceptible nature of knowledge is indicated by darkness. The trumpet also cried out, proclaiming the pleasant sound of the evangelical decrees. God indeed spoke through the voice of the prophets to the Jewish people: I have set watchers over you. Hear the voice of the trumpet. And they said: We will not hear. Therefore, because of this, the nations heard, and the shepherds of the flocks among them listened. Hear, O earth.

The mystery remains veiled, not because it is absent, but because it demands a divine unveiling beyond human reach. Darkness, cloud, and storm are not mere weather but symbols of the hiddenness that surrounds the incarnate Word. Even the prophets' voices, like trumpet blasts, call to attention what the eye cannot see and the heart cannot grasp without heavenly instruction. Those who rely on flesh and blood remain deaf, while those taught by God hear the call. The watchers are set, the trumpet sounds, yet the response is refusal—until the nations turn and listen. So let the earth hear: the mystery calls, and only those given revelation from above can answer.

title: Divine Mystery and the Church
english: As the divine mystery is set upright, twelve stones are placed around it, and calves are sacrificed to initiate the sacred ritual.

At dawn, with morning already breaking and the Daystar shining, the intelligible day dawns for us, night passes, and demonic darkness ceases, allowing the sacred beauty of the Church to shine forth, revealing the altar where the mystery of Christ is completed.
The tribes of the earth stand by, likened to the stones in the examples, as the young men bring the whole burnt offerings and become spiritual priests.
Then, we come into the presence of the Father, standing before Him with our minds ready and prepared for every good thing, making our presence in order.

The divine Paul, tracing the image of the example into reality, writes to those sanctified in Christ, explaining that they are built as living stones into a spiritual house for a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:5).

The divine David clearly prophesied to us, speaking on behalf of those who have believed, saying to the God of all, 'You will hear my voice in the morning', and 'I will stand before you in the morning, and you will see me, for you are not a God who wills lawlessness, nor will a wicked person dwell with you' (Psalm 5:3).

Having been sanctified and purified by blood, Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abiu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up to the mountain, where they saw the work under His feet like sapphire stone, and like the work of the firmament of heaven in purity, and they appeared in the place of God.
None of the chosen of Israel were harmed as they ate and drank in the presence of God.
You hear how they saw the place of God, likened to the firmament of heaven, which is luminous, with an upper and ethereal color like sapphire.

The heaven is a fitting place for God to rest upon, dwelling among angels, for He dwells among holy ones and somehow reclines with those who tread the upper city, because it is very noble and well-prepared for the strength of life.
We believe the multitude of the upper spirits to be holy, and therefore, the things under His feet appeared to those who went up to the mountain like the firmament of heaven in purity.

It was necessary for those who had once been led astray by polytheistic error and had served creation, and then had been called to the knowledge of God, to see that He also has the heaven under His feet, and that He is the Master of all things, as He has brought all things into existence, being the ancient one, and that He is the Master of all things.
